Pepfar-funded HIV organisations in South Africa, who receive their funds through the United States Agency for International Development, USAID, woke up to letters that were sent overnight telling them their grants have been ended - permanently.
Pepfar, the President's Emergency Plan for Aids, is a fund that was launched in 2003 to help fight Aids in countries with high HIV infection rates such as South Africa.
The country has since received around $8 billion (about R145 billion) of which $439 537 828 (about R8.1 billion) was for the current US financial year, which stretches from 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025.
USAID funds 44 health projects in South Africa.
An HIV-positive mother who gave birth to a healthy baby is now at risk of transmitting the virus to her son through breastfeeding.
This mother from Limpopo was part of the Anova programme, one of the largest HIV/Aids projects that had to close overnight after USAID funds almost dried up globally.
The South African mother was in a long-term relationship and needed extensive counselling to accept her HIV status.
She received antiretroviral treatment in Gauteng to reduce her viral load and prevent her baby from contracting HIV, but had to return to Limpopo after losing her job.
Thousands are facing the cold reality of joblessness after the US cut funding to local HIV/Aids organisations – with one LifeLine social worker selling her furniture to make ends meet.
The woman – who asked that her identity be withheld – told News24 she felt as though she was having a panic attack on Thursday when she received the news the grants had been permanently ended.
"My heart is broken," she said.
With unpaid salaries since February and no immediate prospects, she was completing Unemployment Insurance Fund forms when New24 contacted her.
The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria says it will fund the rollout of the twice-yearly anti-HIV jab, lenacapavir, for poorer countries, including South Africa, with or without the help of the US government's AIDS fund, Pepfar.
Pepfar is short for the US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, the fund that US President Donald Trump has halted almost all support for over the past few weeks. "We are still maintaining our ambition on lenacapavir for PrEP," Global Fund executive director, Peter Sands, told Bhekisisa.
"We see lenacapavir as a potential game changer in the fight against HIV as an injectable, long-acting PrEP solution that is pretty well 100% effective. It's not going to be right for everybody, but we need to find out more from having people use it."
In an exclusive interview with News24, renowned epidemiologist Professor Salim Abdool Karim maps the effects of US President Donald Trump's immediate withdrawal of USAID funding for South Africa's HIV/Aids response.
On Thursday morning, USAID-funded organisations and studies received letters from the US government stating their awards were not aligned with American national interests and they should "immediately cease all activities".
Abdool Karim, director of the Centre for the Aids Programme of Research in SA (Caprisa), said the Trump administration's sudden withdrawal was unprecedented but not surprising after a 20 January executive order froze almost all USAID funds around the world pending review.
Abdool Karim has been involved in many studies that were closed down by funders for various reasons; each followed a procedure to smooth the detransition.
First and foremost, the funder gives a warning.
The United States of America's posture of putting its interests first and throwing diplomacy out the window shows that President Donald Trump has upended all sorts of established international relations practices.
This is according to International Crisis Group's senior advisor at the African Union, Liesl Louw-Vaudran.
Louw-Vaudran, an international relations expert, said Trump's "deal-making" style had changed the geopolitical landscape dramatically.
The most recent incident was Friday's meeting between Trump, his deputy JD Vance, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky which descended into a screaming match.
France and Europe will try to fill the gap left by the Trump administration's gutting of USAID, French Deputy Foreign Minister Thani Mohamed-Soilihi has said.
Mohamed-Soilihi, the minister delegate for Francophonie and International Partnerships under the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, akin to a South African deputy minister, spoke to journalists on the sidelines of the Finance in Common Summit (FICS) in Cape Town on Thursday.
The summit, themed "Fostering Infrastructure and Finance for Just and Sustainable Growth", focuses on three pillars: namely inclusive finance, digital transformation, and infrastructure for climate action.
Through a translator, Mohamed-Soilihi said the international situation was grave in terms of solidarity.
South Africa's public health system is in turmoil after the widespread cancellation of USAID funding agreements, reports GroundUp.
Among others, a USAID-funded project that helped to keep orphaned children on their HIV medication was forced to close. HIV testing services are also severely impacted in some areas.
Critical USAID-funded health projects in South Africa were forced to shut down, including some HIV testing and prevention services. This follows the mass termination of contracts globally from 26 February.
One of the affected projects was run by the health non-profit Networking HIV and AIDS Community of Southern Africa (Nacosa).
The Western Cape government has warned that US foreign aid funding cuts may increase the number of HIV/AIDS infections and place more pressure on the province's health system.
This after the Provincial Council on AIDS and TB convened this week to assess the impact of the sudden termination of funding by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) to several non-governmental organisations (NGOs) in the Western Cape.
Chairing the meeting, Premier Alan Winde acknowledged the immediate and significant consequences of this funding halt on NGO partners.
"Our NGO partners play a critical role in supporting our government's response in tackling TB and HIV/AIDS in the Western Cape and South Africa. This abrupt termination of funding has severely disrupted essential services and left many vulnerable residents at risk. This move by the US government is heartbreaking and deeply unfortunate," he said.
The bells are being rung as MPs filter into the dome that now houses the National Assembly chamber.
- Jan Gerber

Two years into the conflict, Sudan’s health system is at breaking point. As the rainy season looms, the country faces a perfect storm of disease outbreaks, malnutrition and collapsing services at a time when humanitarian access is dangerously restricted and funding for health is running dry.
Today, more than 30 million people in Sudan need humanitarian assistance, including over 20 million in urgent need of health services. But insecurity, shortage of life-saving medicines and medical supplies and repeated attacks on health facilities and personnel have made access to care and aid nearly impossible for millions. Hospitals have shut their doors or are only partially functioning. People are dying from diseases, malnutrition, conflict-related injuries and the daily lack of essential medicines, vaccines and lifesaving services.
“This crisis is tearing Sudan’s health system apart,” said WHO Regional Director for the Eastern Mediterranean, Hanan Balkhy. “Hospitals have run out of supplies; health workers are under threat and disease is spreading in areas we can barely reach. The rainy season will multiply the health risks while further restricting access to those in need. We need urgent access and funding to provide essential care to millions of vulnerable people.”
The consequences are already visible. More than two-thirds of Sudan’s states are battling 3 or more disease outbreaks at once, including cholera, dengue, measles and malaria, fuelled by the breakdown of surveillance, vaccinations, clean water systems and vector control. With immunisation campaigns disrupted, children are dying from preventable diseases.
Malnutrition is surging, particularly among young children and mothers. Famine has been confirmed in at least five areas, and projections indicate expansion in 17 areas with 24.6 million people – half the population – expected to face high levels of acute food insecurity in 2025, including 770,000 children under five estimated to suffer from severe acute malnutrition.
Since April 2023, WHO has verified 156 attacks on health care, which have killed 318 people and injured 273. These attacks are blatant violations of international humanitarian law and continue to erode any remaining capacity to deliver care.
Despite these unprecedented constraints, WHO and its partners are doing everything possible to deliver. Since the conflict began, WHO-supported health services have reached over one million patients and helped sustain 52 hospitals across Sudan’s 18 states. More than 10 million children have been vaccinated against measles and rubella, 11.5 million against polio and nearly 12.8 million people against cholera.
Stabilisation centres supported by WHO have treated close to 50,000 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition with medical complications. In November 2024, with WHO support, Sudan launched the malaria vaccine for the first time, targeting 148,000 children in Gedaref and Blue Nile states over a one-year period, more than 35,000 of whom have been vaccinated in the four months since November.
WHO has also expanded support for the clinical management and other lifesaving interventions and mental health and psychosocial support to survivors of gender-based and sexual violence, particularly among displaced populations.
WHO has also delivered over 2,250 metric tons of medical supplies to Sudan’s 18 states since the start of the conflict in April 2023, including via cross-border operations from Chad and South Sudan.
Additionally, WHO’s work with the Ministry of Health in Sudan goes beyond humanitarian support towards development. Recently, the Sudan Health Assistance and Response in Emergencies (SHARE) project was launched, marking a strategic partnership between WHO, the World Bank, the Sudan Ministry of Health, and UNICEF. The project aims to support the emergency, and development needs to restore the functionality of hospitals and primary health centres to provide essential health and nutrition services and support health systems functions.
But the scale of need is still far outpacing the response.
In 2025, WHO has a $135 million-worth response plan, one-fifth of which is funded, only a fraction of what is urgently needed.
“Sudan’s brave health workers are achieving the impossible with almost nothing,” said Dr Balkhy. “They need protection, safe access and the tools to save lives. Time is running out.”
WHO urgently calls on all parties to the conflict in Sudan to ensure unimpeded, sustained humanitarian access and to respect international humanitarian law. Health care is a human right, but in Sudan today it is a lifeline at risk of being severed.

UNICEF has expressed grave concerns about proposed reductions in international aid funding, warning that these cuts could severely impact its ability to provide essential support to millions of vulnerable children worldwide.
The agency highlighted the alarming trend of declining contributions for the second consecutive year, emphasizing that these cuts come at a time when children’s needs are greater than ever.
UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell cautioned, “These reductions will significantly impede our capacity to reach millions of vulnerable children who depend on us for healthcare, vaccines, education, and protection from conflict.”
Despite significant progress in reducing child mortality rates since 2000, UNICEF, which relies entirely on voluntary donations, warns that this funding crisis could jeopardize past achievements and endanger millions more children.
“If these cuts continue, many children may not receive the assistance they need to survive and thrive,” Russell added.
UNICEF urges donors to maintain their support for vital programs, emphasizing the critical need to continue assisting these vulnerable children.

MONROVIA – Liberia’s arguably oldest political party, the Liberian People’s Party (LPP), is clearly picking up steams, increasing its alert and pressure on state institutions found wanting of public expectations and aspirations for greater transparency and accountability. The last time, the political-veterans-studded LPP unleashed a volley of inquiries on another state-owned enterprise, NASSCORP, over its financial deeds, if not misdeeds, particularly since 2014. As The Analyst reports, it seems the LPP, having apparently excavated or suspected fiscal filths, is taking the transparency “war” to the doorsteps of the Liberia Electricity Corporation which has been a key beneficiary of huge national and international largess.
The Liberian People’s Party (LPP) has tendered a strong letter to the Chief Executive Officer
Liberia Electricity Corporation, Monie R. Captan, requesting publish audited financial statements since 2014, grounding the questing in Section 1.1.12 of the 2010 Freedom of Information Act.
The November 4, 2024 letter signed by Chairman J. Yanqui Zaza, the LPP has requested the Liberia Electricity Corporation (LEC) to publish LEC’s audited financial statements of 2015 to 2023 along with schedules of breakdown of the expenditure of the monies it received from Liberia’s development partners.
The LEC-partners’ loans referenced by the LPP include USD$314M loan from the International Development Association; USD$103M from the African Development Bank; LEC’s portion of the USD$257M from the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC); Government of Liberia subsidies and LEC audited financial statements of 2015 to 2023.
The party justified its request to CEO Monie Captan, stating that the Corporation’s publication of its financial statements as prayed for is in accordance with Section 1.1.12 of the 2010 Freedom of Information Act, thereby, providing information on Government’s subsidies allocated in the National Budget covering years; 2017/2018 through 2022/2023 respectively.
According to the LPP, Liberians will fully understand the issue of “Power Theft” at LEC more when they review the Corporation’s financial statements and would help compare the sad story of Power Theft versus the rosy narratives reported by the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA).
“For the years 2015 through 2021,” the party said, quoting official website of the LEC under the management of the Millennium Challenge Account-Liberia, with Monie Captan as the Chief Executive Officer, made a number of feats, including improving reliability of electricity supply more than doubled the number of homes with electricity access; Mount Coffee enabling LEC to expand more reliable and affordable power supply to more than 82,000 homes, businesses, and other entities, compared to a little over 34,000, and the LEC becoming a viable public utility that achieved success in network reliability, availability of power-plants, collection efficiency, new customer connection, and improved customer service.

							By  SAMSON BERHANE ( FORTUNE STAFF WRITER )  							
							
Bidders showed a lack of appetite for the latest auction floated by the National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) to sell 40 billion Br worth of treasury bills.
Tasked with managing securities that will go to finance the government's budget deficit, the central bank received only 14 billion Br in offers during the latest auction, though the weighted average yield (interest) for all classifications of bills exhibited a substantial increase.
It is a disappointing outcome for officials who are desperately looking for funds to narrow the deficit, projected to reach 144 billion Br this year (excluding grants). The tepid interest for the bills is attributed to the disparity between the market interest rate, which has reached as high as 13.5pc in the case of time deposits, and the average yield offered by bidders thus far.
The latest yield recorded for all bills has been the highest since the government liberalised the market at the end of 2019 to enable private entities to buy the security based on market-determined rates.
With 11.6pc yield, the 91-day treasury bill received better offers, accounting for half of the bids received during the latest auction. In contrast, bidders showed less interest in the 364-day treasury bills, buying 1.8 billion Br worth of the security for an average yield of 10.6pc.
The latest central bank report for the second quarter of 2020/21 shows that Ethiopia’s T-bill market, as usual, has been characterised by oversupply.
According to a review carried out by Cepheus Capital a year after authorities liberalised the market, private banks and pension funds supplied the government with close to 95 billion Br in financing – with the highest yield recorded during the same period being 9.3pc for 182-day bills, reaching 10.7pc now.
A market demand of 14.7 billion Br against a supply of 40 billion Br indeed indicates little investor interest.
Political uncertainty, domestic conflict, external pressure, sanctions and delayed debt relief may have played a role in the lack of interest, according to Patrick Heinisch, an economist and capital market researcher.
"This is particularly worrisome as the government plans to resort more frequently to the domestic market to compensate for the loss of budget support that remains suspended by major western donors," he told Fortune.
The federal government hopes to get 66.8 billion Br (1.5 billion dollars at the current exchange rate) in foreign aid to finance its budget deficit for the fiscal year, despite facing backlash from development partners over the humanitarian crisis in Tigray Regional State, where over 854 million dollars is required to feed 5.2 million people who are in need of urgent assistance, according to UN-OCHA.
The ambitious plan surfaced just a month after the parliament approved a 26.4 billion Br supplementary budget due to a gap created by development partners, which officials criticise for having “failed to keep their promises."
For observers and potential bidders, the government, which is likely to face a budget squeeze with surges in expenditure, has to offer better interest on T-bills to grab the attention of more investors. Last year, T-Bills made up nine percent of its domestic debt.
"The low yield on T-bills compared to savings deposits has made investments in T-bills unattractive," remarked Heinisch. That, in fact, was one reason that has pushed the NBE to consider obligating insurers to invest at least 40pc of their admitted assets in T-bills, though this is yet to be implemented.
"We don't want to invest in T-bills as the interest is very low compared to what we get from depositing our money in banks," said Meseret Bezabih, CEO of United Insurance, which had collected 551.2 million Br in premiums from both life and non-life insurance by the end of the third quarter of the just-ended fiscal year.
It seems private banks are also less interested in buying T-bills, which made up roughly four percent of their total lending in December 2020, leaving the government to stick with its age-old buyers: private and public services social security agencies.
"We buy T-bills only if we have excess funds that we don't lend to our customers," said Asfaw Alemu, president of Dashen Bank, whose assets totaled 68.3 billion Br by the end of last year, with an annual profit of 1.5 billion Br.
Asfaw expects demand for the security would further decline as the tax season approaches, particularly during October 2021.
"That is usually a time when we work under tight liquidity conditions," Asfaw added.
For Abdulmenan Mohammed, a financial expert with almost two decades of experience, the lack of interest for the latest T-bill auction could be seasonal.
"As the yield is increasing, banks may even shift to buying T-bills at the expense of customers' borrowing. This, coupled with the strong interest of the government to finance its deficit through T-bills, would further increase the yield for it," he remarked.
The direct advances the federal government took from the central bank saw an 83.4pc annual decline by the end of the last fiscal year, as the government shifted to treasury bills and bonds to finance the budget deficit.
Eyob Tekalign (PhD), state minister for Finance, while defending this year's budget before parliament, affirmed the government's emphasis on T-bills, which he said, is instrumental to curb the inflationary pressure caused by the increase in the money supply.

Bh Siphesihle Dlamini
The Kingdom of Eswatini has taken a decisive step toward combating one of Southern Africa’s most persistent threats: drought. 
At a landmark event held in the serene Ezulwini Valley, aptly called the “valley of heaven,” Prime Minister Russell Dlamini officially launched three vital initiatives aimed at strengthening regional and national resilience to climate-induced disasters.
These initiatives, the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Disaster Risk Reduction Platform, the Eswatini National Platform, and the Eswatini Drought Centre of Excellence, signal a new era of collaboration, innovation, and proactive disaster management across the region.
The Prime Minister opened the event by expressing his profound pride and humility in hosting this historic occasion. He emphasised that the launch reaffirms a collective commitment to “building a safer, resilient, and sustainable future for our region.”
Central to Eswatini’s national strategy is the Nkwe Programme of Action 2024–2029, with a particular focus on Objective 4, which aims to “improve food sovereignty and sustainable development by the year 2029.”
This objective aligns closely with the forum’s theme: “Towards a resilient SADC: advancing regional collaboration and innovation for drought risk management and early warning.”
Dlamini highlighted the urgency of addressing drought, describing it as a “silent crisis” that has historically shaped the region’s development and continues to threaten livelihoods, economies, and ecosystems.
He recalled the devastating 2015–2016 El Niño-induced drought that left nearly half of Eswatini’s population in need of humanitarian assistance.
The economic toll was staggering, with the drought costing approximately E3.84 billion, about 19 per cent of the national budget at the time and 7 per cent of the country’s GDP. This experience underscored the limitations of reactive disaster responses, which are “too costly, both in resources and in human suffering,” prompting the country to shift toward more strategic, long-term resilience building.
In response, Eswatini has adopted a comprehensive approach to drought risk management, prioritising infrastructure and policy reforms. The Prime Minister detailed the
“Eswatini Water Supply and Sanitation Access Project,” financed through a World Bank loan, which improved water access in the drought-prone Shiselweni region.
This initiative integrated water infrastructure, sanitation, and disaster risk management, reflecting a holistic strategy rather than a linear, sector-by-sector approach.
The PM reported that most project deliverables have been achieved or are nearing completion. These include the establishment of water infrastructure, development of risk profiles, municipal drought management plans, and the creation of the Composite Drought Index – Eswatini (CDI-E), a drought monitoring tool.
The National Drought Policy, a key framework integrating drought risk management into the broader development agenda, ensures that “planning, budgeting and implementation across sectors are informed by risk and sustainable efforts.”
Eswatini’s efforts are firmly rooted in global and regional frameworks. The Prime Minister cited the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030), which advocates understanding risk, strengthening governance, investing in resilience, and building back better.
He also referenced the 2015 Paris Agreement’s call to limit global warming while supporting climate adaptation, as well as the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, especially those focused on food security, water management, climate action, and ecosystem preservation.
Regionally, Eswatini aligns with the SADC Disaster Risk Management Strategy and Action Plan 2022, recognising that “only through collective action can we address the shared risks that transcend our borders.”
The launch of the SADC Regional Platform and the Eswatini National Platform represents a tangible step toward these ambitions. According to Dlamini, these platforms will facilitate “dialogue,
coordination, and joint action,” bringing together governments, communities, civil society, the private sector, academia, and development partners to co-create solutions that are “regional in scope but speaking to local realities.” They will also act as conduits for information dissemination and governance enhancement in disaster risk reduction.
A centrepiece of the event was the inauguration of the Eswatini Drought Centre of Excellence, envisioned as a hub for research, policy support, and innovation.
The Centre will leverage science and technology, including climate modelling and early warning systems, while integrating indigenous knowledge and citizen science, which have long been vital to local communities.
By bridging science and practice, the Centre aims to ensure that decisions made at the highest levels are grounded in the realities faced by vulnerable populations.
Dlamini urged the University of Eswatini, the World Bank, and the SADC Secretariat to collaborate closely with the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) to operationalise the Centre for the benefit of the entire African continent.
Acknowledging the critical role of international support, the Prime Minister praised the World Bank Group for helping Eswatini shift its perspective on drought from a mere disaster response issue to a broader development initiative.
He expressed pride in the NDMA’s central role in resilience building, noting that its experience offers valuable lessons for institutions both locally and beyond.
Looking ahead, Dlamini painted a clear vision of the future: one where communities “anticipate risks and respond early and appropriately,” where regional solidarity is not just a principle but a “lived reality,” and where innovation in risk financing, social protection, and water management empowers people to “withstand shocks and continue to thrive in the face of multiple hazards.”
He called on all participants to make the gathering a defining moment, stating, “Let it be said that in Ezulwini, the ‘Valley of Heaven,’ in the Kingdom of Eswatini, we chose to strengthen our resolve, reinforced our partnerships, and raised our ambition.
” He challenged everyone to return home ready to implement the drought risk and resilience assessment methodology.
Concluding with a powerful African proverb, Dlamini reminded the audience: “When the roots are deep, there is no reason to fear the wind.”
His call to action was clear; through unity, commitment, and proactive measures, the region can deepen its roots of resilience and face the future with confidence.

La Force en Attente de la région Afrique de l’Est (EASF) en collaboration avec la République de Djibouti a lancé hier en présence du ministre de l’intérieur M Said Hassan Nouh, un cours sur la Protection des Enfants à l’Académie Idriss Farah Abaneh de la Police Nationale.
L’Académie de Police sise à Nagad a abrité hier la cérémonie d’ouverture d’une formation sur la protection des enfants.
Ce cours qui se déroulera du 04 au 12 novembre, vise à lutter contre la vulnérabilité des enfants et à renforcer les droits des enfants. La formation vise à améliorer la compréhension sur les droits de protection des enfants. Cette session d’apprentissage aidera également les participants à acquérir des connaissances sur leurs rôles et responsabilités dans la protection des enfants dans le contexte des opérations de sécurité et de maintien de la paix.
Cette formation comporte des sessions qui aideront les participants à acquérir de l’expérience, des connaissances et des compétences sur les droits et la protection de l’enfant. La cérémonie d’ouverture a vu la participation du ministre de l’interieurSaidNouh Hassan, de la Procureure Générale de la République Mme Lamis Said, le chef d’État-major de la défense, Général Mohamed Tahiro , du directeur général de la police nationale, Colonel Abdourahman Ali Kahin et du chef d’état-major général de la gendarmerie p.i.
La journée a débuté par un mot de bienvenue du directeur de l’APIFA, le lieutenant-colonel Omar Youssouf qui a d’emblée qualifié l’Académie de Police comme un centre d’excellence régional en matière de formation. Dans la série des discours officiels, le Directeur de l’EASF, le Brigadier Paul KahuriaNjema, s’est félicité du lancement de cette formation au profit des pays membres de l’EASF. Dans son allocution, le directeur de l’EASF a également remercié la République de Djibouti d’avoir permis à l’EASF d’organiser cet important cours.
Le Brigadier Général a poursuivi ses propos en déclarant que la représentation du genre jouait un rôle capital dans ce genre de formation et qu’il était crucial de renforcer leur présence. Signature d’un mémorandum d’entente entre la Police Nationale et la Force en Attente de l’Afrique de l’Est.
A l’issue de cette cérémonie de lancement de formation sur la protection des enfants, le Directeur Général de la police nationale Colonel Abdourahman Ali Kahin et son hôte le Brigadier Paul Njema, Directeur de l’EASF, ont signé un protocole d’entente qui permet de renforcer les formations régionales des personnels de l’EASF au sein de l’Académie de Police. A titre de rappel, la Force en attente de l’Afrique de l’Est (EASF, pour EasternAfrica Standby Force) est une composante régionale de la Force africaine en attente, qui fait partie des initiatives de l’Union Africaine visant à renforcer la capacité de réponse aux crises sur le continent. L’EASF a pour mission de contribuer au maintien de la paix et à la sécurité dans la région de l’Afrique de l’Est. Elle est composée de militaires, de policiers et de civils provenant de dix pays membres, notamment le Kenya, l’Ouganda, le Rwanda, la Somalie, Djibouti, l’Éthiopie, les Seychelles, le Burundi, le Soudan et les Comores. La force peut être déployée rapidement en cas de conflit ou de crise pour des missions telles que le maintien de la paix, la gestion des catastrophes et l’aide humanitaire.
Le cours sur la protection des enfants se poursuivra jusqu’au 12 novembre 2024.
N.Kadassiya
Le point avec :
Le Ministre de l’Intérieur, Said Nouh Hassan
« C’est un honneur de m’exprimer pour la cérémonie de lancement de la formation sur la protection des enfants placée sous le parrainage de l’Eastern Africa Standby Force. Comme vous le savez, la problématique de la protection des enfants est un enjeu crucial pour notre pays mais également pour le monde entier et surtout pour le continent africain. Plus de 60% des habitants ont moins de 30 ans et plus de 200 millions d’enfants se trouvent dans la tranche d’âge de 15 à 24 ans. Il est donc de notre devoir de veiller à leur bien-être et à leur sécurité pour en faire des adultes responsables et soucieux de l’avenir de leur continent. L’objectif de cette formation est de permettre aux participants de s’imprégner des thèmes relatifs à la protection des enfants afin de prévenir ensemble les risques qu’ils peuvent encourir dans un monde en proie à des conflits incessants ».
Colonel Mohamed Aden Barkhad, directeur administratif et financier de l’EASF
« Nous avons signé aujourd’hui un mémorandum d’entente en vue de permettre à l’Académie de Police de devenir un centre de formation pour l’EASF. Comme vous le savez, l’EASF est un mécanisme qui regroupe 10 pays . Djibouti joue un rôle important au sein de cette force. Je voudrais rappeler également que l’académie a déjà abrité d’autre formation de ce genre, mais la particularité aujourd’hui est la signature de ce mémorandum d’entente qui permettra désormais à l’APIFA de s’imposer encore plus comme un centre de formation régional ».
Lieutenant- colonel Omar Youssouf Omar, directeur de l’Académie de Police Idriss Farah Abaneh
« La Police Nationale se réjouit de la signature de ce mémorandum d’entente entre le Directeur de la Police Nationale et le Directeur de l’EASF, qui est une force qui regroupe 10 pays. Il s’agit d’une grande opportunité pour l’académie de Police, qui désormais pourra accueillir les 10 pays de cette force pour y suivre des formations. Il s’agit d’une grande fierté pour notre pays mais aussi pour la Police Nationale. »
Conseiller de Police de l’EASF, M. Langmo Johnny
« Je voudrais remercier tous les états membres de cette force pour leur présence ici. La protection des enfants joue un role important dans le maintien de la paix. Les enfants sont les premières victimes en cas de conflit, d’instabilité ainsi que leurs familles .Le monde fait face à plusieurs challenges et aujourd’hui plus qu’hier, il est important de concentrer nos efforts sur une meilleure coopération. Je voudrais à cet égard rappeler aux pays participants de faire preuve d’assiduité durant cette formation qui porte sur la protection des enfants ».
Propos recueillis par N.Kadassiya

National Police / EASF: Launch of training on Child Protection at the Police Academy

The Eastern Africa Standby Force (EASF), in collaboration with the Republic of Djibouti, launched yesterday, in the presence of the Minister of the Interior Mr Said Hassan Nouh, a course on Child Protection at the Idriss Farah Abaneh Academy of the National Police.

The Police Academy located at Nagad hosted yesterday the opening ceremony of a training course on child protection.

This course, which will run from 4 to 12 November, aims to combat children's vulnerability and to strengthen children's rights. The training aims to improve understanding of child protection rights. This learning session will also help participants acquire knowledge about their roles and responsibilities in protecting children in the context of security and peacekeeping operations.

This training includes sessions that will help participants acquire experience, knowledge and skills on the rights and protection of the child. The opening ceremony was attended by the Minister of the Interior Said Nouh Hassan, the Prosecutor General of the Republic Mrs Lamis Said, the Chief of Defence Staff, General Mohamed Tahiro, the Director General of the National Police, Colonel Abdourahman Ali Kahin, and the acting Chief of Staff of the Gendarmerie.

The day began with a word of welcome from the director of APIFA, Lieutenant-Colonel Omar Youssouf, who from the outset described the Police Academy as a regional centre of excellence in training. In the series of official speeches, the Director of the EASF, Brigadier Paul Kahuria Njema, welcomed the launch of this training for the benefit of EASF member countries. In his address, the EASF director also thanked the Republic of Djibouti for having allowed the EASF to organise this important course.

The Brigadier General continued his remarks by declaring that gender representation played a key role in this kind of training and that it was crucial to strengthen their presence. Signing of a memorandum of understanding between the National Police and the Eastern Africa Standby Force.

At the end of this ceremony launching the training on child protection, the Director General of the national police, Colonel Abdourahman Ali Kahin, and his guest, Brigadier Paul Njema, Director of the EASF, signed a memorandum of understanding that makes it possible to strengthen regional training of EASF personnel within the Police Academy. As a reminder, the Eastern Africa Standby Force (EASF) is a regional component of the African Standby Force, which is part of the African Union's initiatives aimed at strengthening crisis response capacity on the continent. The EASF's mission is to contribute to the maintenance of peace and security in the East Africa region. It is composed of military, police and civilian personnel from ten member countries, notably Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, Somalia, Djibouti, Ethiopia, the Seychelles, Burundi, Sudan and the Comoros. The force can be deployed rapidly in the event of conflict or crisis for missions such as peacekeeping, disaster management and humanitarian aid.

The course on child protection will continue until 12 November 2024.

N. Kadassiya

A word with:

The Minister of the Interior, Said Nouh Hassan
"It is an honour for me to speak at the ceremony launching the training on child protection held under the sponsorship of the Eastern Africa Standby Force. As you know, the issue of child protection is a crucial challenge for our country but also for the whole world and above all for the African continent. More than 60% of inhabitants are under 30 years old and more than 200 million children are in the 15 to 24 age bracket. It is therefore our duty to watch over their well-being and their safety in order to make them responsible adults concerned about the future of their continent. The objective of this training is to allow participants to immerse themselves in themes relating to child protection in order to prevent together the risks they may face in a world beset by incessant conflicts."

Colonel Mohamed Aden Barkhad, administrative and financial director of the EASF
"We signed today a memorandum of understanding with a view to allowing the Police Academy to become a training centre for the EASF. As you know, the EASF is a mechanism bringing together 10 countries. Djibouti plays an important role within this force. I would also like to recall that the academy has already hosted other training of this kind, but the particularity today is the signing of this memorandum of understanding which will henceforth allow APIFA to establish itself even more as a regional training centre."

Lieutenant-Colonel Omar Youssouf Omar, director of the Idriss Farah Abaneh Police Academy
"The National Police welcomes the signing of this memorandum of understanding between the Director of the National Police and the Director of the EASF, which is a force bringing together 10 countries. It is a great opportunity for the Police Academy, which will henceforth be able to host the 10 countries of this force to follow training there. It is a great pride for our country but also for the National Police."

Police Adviser of the EASF, Mr Langmo Johnny
"I would like to thank all the member states of this force for their presence here. Child protection plays an important role in peacekeeping. Children are the first victims in the event of conflict and instability, as are their families. The world faces several challenges and today more than yesterday it is important to concentrate our efforts on better cooperation. I would like in this regard to remind the participating countries to show diligence during this training on child protection."

Remarks collected by N. Kadassiya

Kurs zum Schutz vor Chemiewaffen
Swakopmund/Windhoek (ah/ct) - Der „Kurs zur Übung von Hilfe und Schutz vor chemischen Waffen 2025“ für englischsprachige afrikanische Vertragsstaaten endete am Samstag in Swakopmund mit einem eindringlichen Appell zu regionaler Solidarität und praktischer Einsatzbereitschaft.
Der Kurs in Swakopmund war die vierte Phase des OPCW-Trainingszyklus 2024–2025 für das englischsprachige Afrika und umfasste praktische Demonstrationen, Live-Simulationen sowie eine Abschlussübung. Namibische Behörden und Feuerwehren unterstützten die Übung mit Ausrüstung, während Ausbilder aus Kenia, Namibia, Uganda und Tansania für ihre hochwertige Schulung gewürdigt wurden.
In ihren Abschlussworten betonte Diina Nashidengo, Direktorin für Handel im Ministerium für Industrie, Bergbau und Energie, dass das einwöchige Training „Fokus, Teamarbeit und Engagement“ gefordert habe. Die Teilnehmer gingen „nicht nur mit neuen Fähigkeiten und Wissen, sondern auch mit stärkeren Netzwerken in ganz Afrika“ nach Hause. Nashidengo hob hervor, dass der Kurs die Solidarität zwischen afrikanischen Vertragsstaaten gestärkt habe und rief die Teilnehmer auf, als Botschafter der OPCW ihr Wissen weiterzugeben und Einsatzbereitschaft in ihren Heimatländern zu fördern.
Der OPCW-Programmbeauftragte Babatunde Olowookere erklärte, das Training habe die praktischen Fähigkeiten der Teilnehmer im Umgang mit chemischen Vorfällen gestärkt. Er rief sie auf, dieses Wissen in ihren Einrichtungen weiterzugeben, um den nationalen Kapazitätsaufbau zu fördern.
Nashidengo unterstrich Namibias Stolz, das Programm gemeinsam mit der OPCW auszurichten. Die wiederholte Austragung zeige das Vertrauen in das Land, afrikanische Kapazitäten im Rahmen der Chemiewaffenkonvention zu stärken.
Die OPCW hatte 2023 bestätigt, dass alle deklarierten chemischen Waffenbestände vernichtet wurden, warnte jedoch zugleich vor Selbstzufriedenheit. Afrika gilt als Schwerpunktregion, um die Widerstandsfähigkeit gegen mögliche chemische Bedrohungen durch Terrorismus, Unfälle oder Vorbereitungsdefizite zu erhöhen.
Die Übung in Swakopmund endete mit einem gemeinsamen Bekenntnis zur weiteren Stärkung der regionalen Einsatzbereitschaft. Nashidengo rief die Teilnehmer auf, „weiter für ein sichereres Afrika und eine sicherere Welt zu arbeiten“.

Die Übung in Swakopmund endete mit einem gemeinsamen Bekenntnis zur weiteren Stärkung der regionalen Einsatzbereitschaft. Nashidengo rief die Teilnehmer auf, „weiter für ein sichereres Afrika und eine sicherere Welt zu arbeiten“.

a598.en:
Course on protection against chemical weapons

Swakopmund/Windhoek (ah/ct) - The "Course on the Practice of Assistance and Protection against Chemical Weapons 2025" for English-speaking African States Parties ended on Saturday in Swakopmund with an urgent appeal for regional solidarity and practical operational readiness.

The course in Swakopmund was the fourth phase of the OPCW training cycle 2024-2025 for English-speaking Africa and included practical demonstrations, live simulations and a final exercise. Namibian authorities and fire services supported the exercise with equipment, while instructors from Kenya, Namibia, Uganda and Tanzania were commended for their high-quality training.

In her closing remarks, Diina Nashidengo, Director of Trade in the Ministry of Industry, Mines and Energy, stressed that the week-long training had demanded "focus, teamwork and commitment". Participants went home "not only with new skills and knowledge, but also with stronger networks across Africa". Nashidengo emphasised that the course had strengthened solidarity among African States Parties and called on the participants to pass on their knowledge as ambassadors of the OPCW and to promote operational readiness in their home countries.

OPCW programme officer Babatunde Olowookere explained that the training had strengthened participants' practical skills in dealing with chemical incidents. He called on them to pass this knowledge on within their institutions in order to promote national capacity-building.

Nashidengo underlined Namibia's pride in co-hosting the programme together with the OPCW. Hosting it repeatedly showed the confidence placed in the country to strengthen African capacities within the framework of the Chemical Weapons Convention.

In 2023 the OPCW had confirmed that all declared chemical weapons stockpiles had been destroyed, but at the same time warned against complacency. Africa is regarded as a priority region for increasing resilience against possible chemical threats arising from terrorism, accidents or preparedness gaps.

The exercise in Swakopmund ended with a joint commitment to further strengthening regional operational readiness. Nashidengo called on the participants to "keep working for a safer Africa and a safer world".

a772.t:
Le milliardaire propriétaire de Tesla et de X est désormais à la tête d'un département où il peut faire ce que bon lui semble.
Après s'être rapproché de Donald Trump, Elon Musk a désormais la main sur les finances de l'Etat américain. Le milliardaire, qui est aussi le patron de grandes entreprises comme Tesla et SpaceX, mais aussi du réseau social X, n'en finit plus de faire la pluie et le beau temps sur les économies à réaliser au sein de l'état fédéral.
Une situation qui a alerté le groupe de défense des droits des citoyens, Public Citizen, qui a fait un appel à un tribunal fédéral de Washington pour mettre fin, selon lui, aux "divulgations illégales, systématiques et continues d'informations personnelles et financières" de la part d'Elon Musk ou d'autres membres du "Département de l'efficacité gouvernementale" (Doge).
Grâce au Doge, Elon Musk et ses équipes aurait eu accès aux numéros de sécurité sociale et aux données personnelles de millions d'Américains, ce qui violerait la loi sur la protection de la vie privée de 1974, mais aussi celle concernant le secret des contribuables.
Selon le site Wired, le patron de Tesla, X et SpaceX a ainsi placé des jeunes gens travaillant pour le Doge à des postes gouvernementaux clés. Ces équipes ont désormais un accès sans précédent au système de paiements, normalement la chasse gardée de hauts fonctionnaires apolitiques.
De graves conflits d'intérêts
Une décision autorisée par le Trésor américain, représenté par Scott Bessent, afin de réduire drastiquement les budgets alloués par le gouvernement. Elon Musk, qui cherchait à passer la dépense publique de 7.000 milliards de dollars à 2.000 milliards de dollars, vise désormais plutôt les 3.500 milliards de dollars. Pour ce faire, il a activement tranché dans les financements alloués au Planning familial, qui informe les personnes sur l'avortement ou les moyens de contraception. Les programmes pour les minorités ont aussi été supprimés ou réduits.
Dernièrement, c'est l'aide américaine au développement, à destination des pays les plus pauvres du monde, l'USAID, qui a été effacée des radars sans autre forme de procès.
Cette petite révolution n'est en tout cas pas du goût des sénateurs démocrates. La sénatrice démocrate Elizabeth Warren, membre de la commission bancaire du Sénat, a qualifié la situation "d'extrêmement dangereuse" dans une lettre à Scott Bessent.
Ron Wyden, qui représente l'Oregon, a expliqué qu'Elon Musk représentait un risque pour la sécurité nationale, en raison de l'accès illimité à certaines données financières. En outre le syndicat des employés du gouvernement fédéral a également lancé l'alerte afin de rappeler les textes de loi en vigueur, et qui oblige normalement des garde-fous.
De son côté, l'ex-colistier de Kamala Harris, Tim Waltz, a critiqué le milliardaire qui semble prendre un poids considérable dans l'administration américaine : "Elon Musk est un président terrible" a-t-il écrit.
Seul aux commandes du DOGE, Elon Musk est également accusé de graves conflits d'intérêts. Il peut en effet saborder le budget fédéral à l'envie, en fonction de ses propres entreprises, mais aussi de ses desseins politiques. Depuis plusieurs semaines, il multiplie les incartades sur son réseau social X, appelant notamment à voter pour le parti d'extrême droite allemand AfD et critiquant vertement le Premier ministre anglais.
Sylvain Trinel
Source: https://www.bfmtv.com/
a772.en:
"Elon Musk is a terrible president": the power seized by the billionaire worries the Democratic opposition

The billionaire owner of Tesla and X is now at the head of a department where he can do as he pleases.

After growing close to Donald Trump, Elon Musk now has his hands on the finances of the American state. The billionaire, who is also the boss of large companies such as Tesla and SpaceX, as well as of the social network X, never stops calling the shots on the savings to be made within the federal state.

A situation that has alarmed the citizens' rights advocacy group Public Citizen, which has appealed to a federal court in Washington to put an end to what it calls the "illegal, systematic and ongoing disclosures of personal and financial information" by Elon Musk or other members of the "Department of Government Efficiency" (Doge).

Thanks to Doge, Elon Musk and his teams are said to have gained access to the social security numbers and personal data of millions of Americans, which would violate the 1974 privacy law, as well as the law on taxpayer confidentiality.

According to the website Wired, the boss of Tesla, X and SpaceX has thus placed young people working for Doge in key government positions. These teams now have unprecedented access to the payments system, normally the preserve of apolitical senior civil servants.

Serious conflicts of interest

A decision authorised by the US Treasury, represented by Scott Bessent, in order to drastically reduce the budgets allocated by the government. Elon Musk, who was seeking to cut public spending from 7,000 billion dollars to 2,000 billion dollars, is now targeting rather 3,500 billion dollars. To do so, he has actively slashed the funding allocated to Planned Parenthood, which informs people about abortion or means of contraception. Programmes for minorities have also been eliminated or reduced.

Most recently, it is American development aid, intended for the poorest countries in the world, USAID, that has been wiped off the radar without further ado.

This little revolution is in any case not to the taste of Democratic senators. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, described the situation as "extremely dangerous" in a letter to Scott Bessent.

Ron Wyden, who represents Oregon, explained that Elon Musk represented a national security risk, because of his unlimited access to certain financial data. In addition, the federal government employees' union also sounded the alarm in order to recall the laws in force, which normally require safeguards.

For his part, Kamala Harris's former running mate, Tim Waltz, criticised the billionaire who appears to be taking on considerable weight in the American administration: "Elon Musk is a terrible president," he wrote.

Alone at the controls of DOGE, Elon Musk is also accused of serious conflicts of interest. He can indeed scuttle the federal budget at will, according to his own companies' interests, but also his political designs. For several weeks, he has been multiplying his provocations on his social network X, notably calling for a vote for the German far-right party AfD and sharply criticising the British Prime Minister.

Sylvain Trinel
Source: https://www.bfmtv.com/
